title: Quantum Computing Applications in Financial Modeling and Portfolio Optimization
journal_or_venue: 2025 First International Conference on Advances in Computer Science, Electrical, Electronics, and Communication Technologies (CE2CT)
abstract_summary: The paper examines applications of quantum computing for financial modeling and portfolio optimization, presenting a QUBO formulation and a banking loan portfolio case study that includes emissions and risk constraints. It compares classical convex optimization, simulated annealing, and quantum annealing approaches, reporting that simulated annealing outperformed quantum annealing in their experiments while discussing opportunities and practical challenges for implementing quantum algorithms on near-term hardware.
methodology_description: The study formulates a portfolio optimization problem over a set of assets (loans) characterized by expected returns and a covariance (risk) matrix, includes binary decision variables to indicate asset selection and enforces constraints including bounds per asset and an emissions (CO2 intensity) constraint. The continuous/mixed problem is converted to a QUBO representation for combinatorial solving. As benchmarks and baselines the authors (a) solve a convex quadratic formulation using classical convex optimization (linear matrix inequality solved with SeDuMi via the Matlab–YALMIP toolbox) to obtain Pareto frontiers, (b) generate a large random sample of feasible binary portfolios (each asset set to lower or upper bound) and (c) apply probabilistic annealing methods on the QUBO formulation — specifically simulated annealing — and compare the results qualitatively to quantum annealing. Visualization of random samples and Pareto frontiers is used to compare solution quality. The paper reports qualitative findings that simulated annealing produced solutions closer to the Pareto frontier than the quantum annealing approach in their experiments. The methodology includes a provided pseudocode for a convex optimization routine and a QUBO formulation embedding the emission constraint as penalty terms.
algorithms_used: Quantum annealing (compared but not detailed experimentally)
dataset_used: A banking case-study portfolio of outstanding loans as of 2021; objective is to reallocate across countries/subsectors/industry to a target composition for 2030 while balancing return, risk and CO2 emission intensity. No public dataset source, size, or detailed asset list is provided in the paper.
experiment_process: 1) Define assets, expected returns vector and covariance (risk) matrix; include binary decision variables and bounds per asset. 2) Encode objectives (maximize return, minimize risk) and emission constraints; form an augmented objective with penalties and derive a QUBO representation of the constrained problem. 3) Solve classical convex variant (quadratic program / LMI) using SeDuMi via Matlab-YALMIP to obtain Pareto frontier(s). 4) Generate a random sample of binary portfolios by setting each asset either to its lower or upper bound (reported sample size: 252,252 combinations). 5) Apply simulated annealing to the QUBO to search for high-quality solutions; accept/reject moves probabilistically (standard simulated annealing paradigm). 6) Compare the simulated-annealing solutions qualitatively to outcomes reported from quantum annealing runs (quantum annealer solver details not specified). 7) Visualize sampled portfolios and Pareto frontiers to assess proximity of solutions to Pareto-optimal set. Note: the paper gives a convex optimization pseudocode but does not supply numerical hyperparameters for the annealing schedules, temperatures, number of iterations, or solver tolerances.
experiment_output: Outputs reported are Pareto frontier plots and scatter visualizations of sampled portfolios (colored dots for random samples and markers for Pareto frontiers). The study reports the number of sampled solutions (252,252) and a qualitative comparison: simulated annealing produced solutions closer to the (classical) Pareto frontier than quantum annealing in their tests. No formal numeric metrics (e.g., objective distances, runtimes, statistical tests) or tabulated performance numbers are provided.

results_summary: The paper formulates a constrained portfolio optimization (loans portfolio with CO2 emission and allocation constraints) as a QUBO and compares solution methods. Classical convex optimization (via SeDuMi/YALMIP) is used to obtain Pareto-front baselines. The authors performed sampling and optimization experiments and report that, for their instance, simulated annealing (classical) outperformed the applied quantum annealing technique in approaching the Pareto frontier and yielded a wider diversity of feasible solutions. The paper emphasizes theoretical benefits and application areas for quantum computing in finance but does not provide empirical demonstrations of quantum advantage; it also cites prior empirical findings that certain quantum-annealer parameters (chain strength, number of reads) materially affect results.
performance_claims: 252,252 — number of solutions produced by the naive binary-sampling approach described for the 2030 portfolio scenario.
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper does not demonstrate a quantum computational advantage; in the reported experiments a classical optimizer (simulated annealing) outperformed the applied quantum annealing approach on the presented portfolio QUBO instance. Broader claims about future quantum benefits for finance are speculative and not empirically shown in this work.

An apparent statement in the introduction that 'classical computers can surpass the computational power anticipated using quantum computers' contradicts standard literature framing that quantum computers can offer asymptotic or practical advantages for some problems; this appears to be an internal inconsistency or misstatement in the paper.
